**Purpose** — Templates give you a working starting point. Instead of configuring an application or Compose stack from scratch, you deploy a blueprint and adapt it, or follow an example that matches your framework.

## Two kinds of starting point

| | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| **Templates gallery** | You want a ready-made Compose stack for a known open-source app (databases, CMS, analytics, tools). |
| **Framework examples** | You are deploying your own application and want the recommended settings for its framework. |

## Templates gallery

The [Notploy Templates gallery](https://templates.notploy.com) is a catalogue of more than 500 one-click open-source blueprints. Each blueprint ships a Docker Compose definition plus a small configuration that tells Notploy which secrets to generate, which domains to route and which files to mount, so you can stand up a service without authoring the compose file yourself.

Deploy one straight from a project environment:

1. **Create Service → Template** — search the catalogue.
2. **Create** — Notploy builds a Compose service from the blueprint.
3. **Deploy** — open the generated domain.

→ Full walkthrough in [Templates gallery](/docs/templates/gallery)

<Callout type="info">
Templates deploy as [Docker Compose](/docs/core/docker-compose) services. Once deployed, they behave like
any other Compose stack — you can edit the compose file, set variables and add domains.
</Callout>

## Anatomy of a blueprint

Every blueprint is a self-contained folder under `templates/blueprints/` in the Notploy repository. Four pieces make it work:

| Piece | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `docker-compose.yml` | The stack Notploy deploys. |
| `template.toml` | Variables, environment, domains and file mounts resolved when the service is created. |
| `meta.json` + logo | Catalogue metadata: name, version, description, links and tags. |
| `instructions.md` | Optional setup guide shown in the gallery. |

## Framework examples

Examples show how to deploy common frameworks on Notploy, including the recommended **build type** and any framework-specific settings (for example the port to expose, or a build command). They are reference pages, not files you deploy directly.
